title: Children and rehat
hookLine: the code says amrit may be taken when one is old enough to understand

lines: A CROOKED KNOT, A LATE STAND.
HE KNOWS THE WORDS, NOT YET THE MEANING.
WHEN DOES THE QUESTION GET ASKED?
cards: A small boy in a gurdwara sits beside his father, a tiny patka on his head, the knot slightly crooked.
During the Ardas he stands when everyone stands, a beat late, and folds his hands because his father's hands are folded. He knows some of the words. He doesn't yet know what most of them mean.
Is he keeping the rehat? Is he a Sikh yet? The Sikh code has an answer about when the big question gets asked, and it isn't a number on a birthday card.

teach.h: THE CODE: OLD ENOUGH TO UNDERSTAND.
teach.b: In the Rehat Maryada's section on amrit, the code says, in paraphrase, that the one being initiated should not be very young, and should have reached an age of understanding.
Notice what it doesn't say: there's no number. The measure is understanding. Why?

Think of what the initiate is told at amrit: the daily banis, the five articles, the four things never to do. Those are promises, and a promise only means something when the person making it knows what's being promised.
Early on, this path called amrit a step, not a pressure. So amrit waits. But waiting isn't leaving the child outside.

teach.h: NAMED BEFORE THE GURU, RAISED INSIDE.
teach.b: Earlier in this block you met the naming, where a hukam is taken from the Guru Granth Sahib and the child's name begins with the first letter of that hymn. From the start, the child is brought into the Guru's presence.

In families who keep the code, a child's hair is left uncut long before any vow, and the child grows up hearing Japji in the morning and Kirtan Sohila at night, sitting cross-legged in the langar line.
That's how a child reaches understanding: not by being told every rule at once, but by living inside the practice first.
Some families teach Gurmukhi, the script of the Granth, so the child can read the hymns for themselves. And there's a quiet respect in this.

teach.h: THE GROUND PREPARED, THE CHOICE KEPT.
teach.b: The code doesn't take the choice away by making it too early. It prepares the ground, and waits for the child to step forward on their own.

how: Sikh children are named in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib and raised with the daily prayers; the Rehat Maryada says amrit should be taken when one is old enough to understand, without setting an age.

o: children take amrit at a fixed age, like thirteen
children may not enter a gurdwara until initiated
amrit waits until a child can understand the vow

games.q: a young child asks to take amrit with an older cousin. what does the code point to?
o: any age is fine if the parents agree.
wait until the child is old enough to understand.
amrit is only for adults over a set age.
games.why: the code sets no number. it asks that the initiate not be very young, and have reached understanding, because amrit is a promise.

practice: Think of one rule you keep and how you'd explain it to a child in two sentences, without saying because I said so; if there's no child in your life, explain it to the child you once were.
Find the simplest true reason, and say it to yourself once. Then breathe, and notice whether finding it changed how you hold the rule.

wordCard.voice: Children and rehat. The Sikh code says amrit is not for the very young: one should be old enough to understand. Until then, children are named before the Guru and raised inside the practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: understanding, sense. the code's measure for amrit is understanding, not a set age.

carryVoice: Your line: when they understand. A promise means most when it's understood. See you tomorrow.
